title: Circling the Garage
story: A camera at a parking garage entrance logs the plate of every car that drives in, in order. A driver who finds no free spot leaves by the exit ramp and often comes straight back in.
The manager wants to detect this, which means finding the same plate entering twice within a few log entries. The same car returning hours later is a normal visit and does not count as circling.
task: Write circlingCar(plates, k). Return true if there are two positions i < j with plates[i] === plates[j] and j - i ≤ k. Otherwise return false.
An empty log returns false. With k = 0 no pair can qualify, so the answer is false.

examples.explanation: Plate 77 entered at positions 1 and 3. The gap is 3 - 1 = 2, which is within k = 2, so the answer is true.
Plate 512 entered at 0 and 4. 4 - 0 = 4 is more than k = 3, so that was a normal second visit. No other plate repeats, so the answer is false.
Plate 8 entered at positions 0, 4 and 6. The gaps from the first visit, 4 and 6, are too big, but the visits at positions 4 and 6 are only 2 apart, so the answer is true.

hints: In [3, 9, 3] with k = 2, the 3s are at positions 0 and 2. At position 2, what single fact about plate 3 do you need from the past?
Only the most recent earlier visit matters. If it is too far back, every older visit is further still.
Keep one number per plate: the position where you last saw it. Which structure gives you that in one step?
Walk the log with a map from plate to last position. At each position j, if the plate is in the map and j - last ≤ k, return true. Either way, update the map to j. Return false at the end.
bruteForce: Compare each entry with the next k entries and return true on a match.
That is about n × k comparisons: billions with 100,000 entries and k = 100,000. Each entry rescans cars that earlier entries already looked at.

js: * @param {number[]} plates  plate numbers in entry order
* @param {number} k  the largest gap that still counts as circling
py: def circling_car(plates: list[int], k: int) -> bool:

tests.note: a repeat exists but too far apart: defeats plain duplicate checks
only the latest visit is close: defeats keeping the first position

js: const last = new Map(); // plate -> position of its latest entry
if (last.has(plates[j]) && j - last.get(plates[j]) <= k) return true;
last.set(plates[j], j); // this is now the latest visit
py: last = {}  # plate -> position of its latest entry
if plate in last and j - last[plate] <= k:
last[plate] = j  # this is now the latest visit
walkthrough: This is the duplicate check from Double-Scanned Tickets with a distance limit. A set is no longer enough: you need where you last saw a plate, so store the position.
• At positions 0 to 3 the plates 8, 1, 2 and 3 are all new, so the map becomes 8 → 0, 1 → 1, 2 → 2, 3 → 3.
• At position 4 the plate is 8, last seen at position 0. The gap is 4, which is greater than 2, so this is not circling, and the map entry for 8 is updated to 4.
• At position 5 the plate is 4, which is new, so the map gets 4 → 5.
• At position 6 the plate is 8, last seen at position 4. The gap is 2, which is within k, so the function returns true.
The update in step 2 is the important line. If the map kept the first position, 8 → 0, the last visit would see a gap of 6 and the function would wrongly return false.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, and each map lookup or update is O(1) on average.
solution.spaceWhy: With no repeats the map ends up holding every plate. Keeping only the last k plates in a set would cut this to O(k).
solution.takeaway: When a match only counts if it is close enough, store each value's latest position in a hash map, not just whether you saw it. The most recent occurrence is always the best candidate.
